lessons.title: Pre-colonial states and societies

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the main West African empires and their trade
Describe states and societies in Cameroon before colonial rule
Identify the features of centralised and decentralised societies
reviewNotes: Verify: Ghana c. 8th–11th century; Mali c. 13th–15th; Songhai 15th–16th; Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage c. 1324; defeat of Songhai 1591; Sokoto jihad 1804.
Check how the syllabus presents Cameroon’s pre-colonial peoples (Duala, Bamum, Fulbe, Tikar, Bamileke).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The Sahelian empires
blocks.md: Gold, salt, cloth, ivory and slaves crossed the Sahara by camel caravan. Control of this **trans-Saharan trade** made three successive empires powerful: **Ghana** (from about the 8th to the 11th century), **Mali** (about the 13th to 15th century) and **Songhai** (15th–16th century), with centres such as Gao and Timbuktu famous for trade and Islamic learning. Mansa Musa of Mali made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in about 1324. Songhai was defeated by a Moroccan army in 1591.

blocks.title: Lake Chad region and the forest
blocks.md: **Kanem-Bornu**, near Lake Chad, was a long-lived state controlling trans-Saharan routes. In the forest and coastal zones, states such as Oyo and Benin and, later, Asante had kings, councils, armies and trading networks. Societies without kings, organised by age sets, lineages and councils, also existed.

blocks.caption: Approximate periods of three West African empires.
blocks.alt: A timeline from 700 to 1700 showing Ghana, Mali and Songhai periods, and the dates 1324 and 1591.

blocks.title: Cameroon
blocks.md: The **Bamum** kingdom with its capital at Foumban and the chiefdoms (fondoms) of the western grassfields, such as many Bamileke and Tikar groups, were organised states under rulers with courts and titled officials. In the north, Fulbe (Fulani) emirates were founded in the 19th century after the jihad movement led from Sokoto (1804). On the coast, the **Duala** acted as middlemen in trade with Europeans. Each had its own politics, economy and culture.

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- Africa had complex states and societies long before European rule.
- Do not treat empires as having fixed modern borders: control was strongest near centres and trade routes.
- Dates for early empires are approximate; use ‘about’ or ‘c.’ unless you are certain.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Why trade made Mali wealthy
blocks.statement: Explain why control of the trans-Saharan trade made the Mali empire rich.
steps: Gold came from the south and salt from the Sahara; both were in high demand.
Mali’s rulers taxed caravans and traders passing through their lands.
Wealth paid for armies, cities and pilgrimage, strengthening the state.
blocks.answer: Taxing the gold-salt trade gave revenue and power.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Compare two types of society
blocks.statement: Compare a centralised kingdom with a society ruled by councils and age sets.
steps: Kingdom: a ruler, court and titled officials, taxes and an army.
Council-based society: decisions by elders and councils, authority shared through lineage and age-grade.
Both had laws and ways to settle disputes.
blocks.answer: Centralised authority versus shared authority; both organised.

lessons.title: The trans-Atlantic slave trade and its abolition
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board, Advanced Level History syllabus (Lower Sixth) — to be checked against the official text

objectives: Describe the origins, organisation and effects of the trans-Atlantic slave trade
Describe the settlement of freed slaves and the shift to ‘legitimate trade’
reviewNotes: Verify: 1807 Slave Trade Act; 1833 Slavery Abolition Act (effective 1834); France 1848; USA 1865; Victoria founded 1858; Saker’s activities; ‘more than ten million’ is a rounded scholarly estimate.
Teach this topic sensitively; follow the official syllabus emphasis.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The trade
blocks.md: From the 15th century European traders carried captive Africans to work on plantations in the Americas. More than ten million people were taken across the Atlantic in over three centuries, most in the 18th century. The **triangular trade** linked Europe (manufactured goods), Africa (captives) and the Americas (sugar, cotton, tobacco). African rulers and merchants took part in the trade, which was enforced by European demand and by the guns and goods offered.

blocks.title: Effects
blocks.md: **On Africa:** loss of many young people, insecurity and wars to capture people, damaged societies and economies in affected regions; some states grew powerful by controlling the trade. **In the Americas:** forced labour and the growth of plantation economies and large African-descended populations. **In Europe:** profits for traders and ports, which helped finance later development.

blocks.caption: Slave trade and abolition dates.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1500 to 1900 with the trans-Atlantic slave trade period and abolition dates 1807, 1833 and 1848.

blocks.title: Abolition
blocks.md: Causes: the campaigns of abolitionists (including freed Africans such as Olaudah Equiano), religious and humanitarian movements, resistance and revolt by enslaved people, and changing economic interests in Britain. **Britain banned the slave trade in 1807** and abolished slavery in most of its empire in **1833** (effective 1834). The Royal Navy patrolled West African waters. France abolished slavery finally in 1848; the United States in 1865.

blocks.title: After abolition
blocks.md: Settlements for freed people were founded, including Freetown in Sierra Leone and Liberia. Europeans promoted **‘legitimate trade’** in palm oil, groundnuts and rubber instead of people. On the Cameroon coast, Duala and other coastal communities traded palm oil and the missions, such as the Baptist mission under Alfred Saker, established Victoria (now Limbe) in 1858 as a settlement for freed people.

blocks.title: Handle with care
blocks.md:
- The trade was driven by European demand but African participation varied by region and period; avoid blaming one group.
- Abolition of the trade (1807) is not the same as the end of slavery (1833 and later).
- Slavery and the slave trade continued in some places after abolition laws.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Triangular trade
blocks.statement: Describe the three sides of the triangular trade.
steps: Europe to Africa: manufactured goods, guns, cloth.
Africa to the Americas: captive Africans (the Middle Passage).
Americas to Europe: sugar, cotton, tobacco and other plantation goods.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why abolish?
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807.
steps: Humanitarian campaigns by abolitionists and churches changed opinion.
Resistance and revolts by enslaved people raised the cost and risk.
Economic interests were shifting, and some argued other trade would pay better.

objectives: Describe the roles of explorers, missionaries and traders
Explain how the coast of Cameroon attracted European interest
Assess the link between these groups and colonial conquest
reviewNotes: Verify: Park 1790s; Landers 1830; Nachtigal treaty with Duala chiefs July 1884 (12 July is often given); Duala letters to Britain in the 1870s; Saker, Merrick and the Baptist mission; Basel Mission arrival 1886.
Check the names used for Duala rulers (Bell, Akwa) as in the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Explorers
blocks.md: In the 19th century European explorers travelled in Africa to map rivers and routes: **Mungo Park** on the Niger (1790s), the **Lander brothers** (1830, the mouth of the Niger), **Heinrich Barth** in the Sahel and Lake Chad region, and **David Livingstone** in central and southern Africa. Their reports gave information about peoples, resources and routes, and increased European interest.

blocks.title: Missionaries
blocks.md: Missionaries built churches, schools and clinics. Baptist missionaries such as Joseph Merrick and Alfred Saker worked on the Cameroon coast from the 1840s; the Basel Mission, Catholic missions and others followed. They translated the Bible, taught reading, and introduced new ideas, but they also sometimes prepared the way for colonial rule. Africans took many of the teaching roles.

items.text: Treaties and claims lead to colonial rule

blocks.caption: How contact led to colonial rule (simplified).
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a chain: explorers, missionaries and traders, rivalry, and treaties leading to colonial rule.

blocks.title: Traders and treaties
blocks.md: European traders from Britain and Germany bought palm oil, ivory and rubber at the Cameroon coast. Duala rulers, such as King Bell and King Akwa, controlled the trade and in the 1870s sent letters to Britain asking for protection and a settlement of their affairs. In July 1884, German representative Gustav Nachtigal signed treaties with the Duala chiefs, beginning German rule. Many details are debated by historians.

blocks.title: Be balanced
blocks.md: Explorers, missionaries and traders were not all the same: some respected African societies, others did not. Africans were not passive; they used trade and diplomacy to defend their interests. Avoid saying that missionaries were only agents of colonialism or only helpers of Africans.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Importance of explorers
blocks.statement: Explain why explorers’ reports increased European interest in Africa.
steps: They described rivers and routes into the interior, showing how to reach inland markets.
They described resources such as gold, ivory and palm oil.
Their books were popular and increased public interest at home.
blocks.answer: Information and publicity encouraged commercial and political interest.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Role of missionaries
blocks.statement: Give two positive and one critical point about the work of missionaries in Cameroon’s coast.
steps: Positive: schools taught reading and writing; the Bible was translated into local languages.
Positive: clinics and new skills were introduced.
Critical: the missions sometimes undermined local religion and customs and supported colonial authority.
blocks.answer: A mixed record that needs balanced treatment.
